title: Lesson Feedback: Don't Send It, Don't Give It - Co-Construct It. Otherwise, It Won't Be Worth It erwise-it-wont-be-worth-it/
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington makes a blunt case against written or emailed lesson-observation feedback, arguing that however well-intentioned, it is a leftover of old school top-down leadership that mostly serves the observer's own sense of professional competence rather than the teacher's actual development. Drawing on his own past as a school leader who spent "wasted, pointless hours" crafting polished observation reports, he now argues that presuming to tell a teacher what they did wrong from a single 10-20 minute snapshot is fundamentally disrespectful, given how biased and partial any observer's insight necessarily is compared to what the teacher lives through in the classroom every day. His alternative is co-construction: an observer should walk into a lesson only gathering material for a subsequent conversation, then use that conversation to help the teacher generate their own insight and next steps rather than receiving a verdict. He's explicit that feedback which the teacher didn't help generate is functionally redundant even when accurate, since the value lies in the teacher's own understanding and buy-in, not the correctness of the observer's read. Sherrington ties the argument to teacher retention, framing a scrutiny-based, drop-in-and-report culture as directly corrosive to the supportive, reflective professional culture schools need to keep staff.
points: Sherrington's core reversal is that written or emailed lesson observation feedback primarily serves the observer's ego ("a job well done"), not the teacher's development, regardless of how well-crafted the report is.

He argues observer insight is inherently limited and biased - present for 10-20 minutes against a teacher's near-total autonomy the rest of the time - which should produce humility rather than confident top-down verdicts.

His replacement principle is co-construction: feedback only becomes real when the teacher generates the action themselves in conversation, using the observer's insight as raw material rather than a finished verdict.

Sherrington connects the practice to teacher retention, arguing scrutiny-driven, drop-in written feedback culture is directly at odds with building a supportive professional learning culture at a moment when retention is under strain.
quotes: Don’t you dare walk into my classroom for 10-20 minutes, with all your status and biases and then presume to write to me or to just tell me what I could have done better! Like you just ‘know’.

When you watch a lesson it’s important to acknowledge and respect the fact that, not only are your insights steeped in biases and fragile assumptions, the teacher is going to be doing what they do all by themselves 99% of the time -without any input from you at all.
When you meet the teacher, you then use the insights gained from your observation to support the teacher in their professional process. It’s theirs, not yours.

The only feedback that matters has lead to concrete actions a teacher actually takes. A teacher can’t merely receive feedback; they have to generate it themselves, taking account of the observer’s offerings.
The person who gets the most from writing a lesson observation comment or report is the observer – it satisfies their professional ego; their sense of a job well done. But that’s not the point is it?
So, I’ll say it again: Lesson feedback: don’t send it, don’t give it – co-construct it. Otherwise, it won’t be worth it.
